== Problem ==
What is the greatest three-digit positive integer <imath>n</imath> for which the sum of the first <imath>n</imath> positive integers is <imath>\underline{\text{not}}</imath> a divisor of the product of the first <imath>n</imath> positive integers?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 995 \qquad\textbf{(B) } 996 \qquad\textbf{(C) } 997 \qquad\textbf{(D) } 998 \qquad\textbf{(E) } 999</imath>

== Solutions ==
=== Solution 1 ===
The sum of the first <math>n</math> positive integers is <math>\frac{(n)(n+1)}{2}</math>, and we want this to not be a divisor of <math>n!</math> (the product of the first <math>n</math> positive integers). Notice that if and only if <math>n+1</math> were composite, all of its factors would be less than or equal to <math>n</math>, which means they would be able to cancel with the factors in <math>n!</math>. Thus, the sum of <math>n</math> positive integers would be a divisor of <math>n!</math> when <math>n+1</math> is composite. (Note: This is true for all positive integers except for 1 because 2 is not a divisor/factor of 1.) Hence in this case, <math>n+1</math> must instead be prime. The greatest three-digit integer that is prime is <math>997</math>, so we subtract <math>1</math> to get <math>n=\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 996}</math>.

===Solution 1.1===
The sum of the first \( n \) positive integers starting from 1 is \( \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \). The product of the first \( n \) positive integers starting from \( n \), then going to \( (n-1) \), all the way down to 1, is \( n! \). If there exists a number such that \( n! / \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = +\mathbb{Z} \), then we call that solution invalid. \( n! / \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \) is just \( \frac{2n!}{n(n+1)} \). We see that the first term of \( n! \), which is \( n \), will cancel out with the \( n \) term on the denominator. In order for \( n-1 \) to not cancel out, it needs to be a prime number. The only answer choice that satisfies this <math>n=\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 996}</math>.

~Pinotation (not the creator of Solution 1)

=== Solution 2 (easier answer choice elimination)===
As in Solution 1, we deduce that <math>n+1</math> must be prime. 

It's hard to remember all of your primes up to a thousand, so we eliminate answer choices
choices <math>A</math>, <math>C</math>, and <math>E</math> don't work because <math>n+1</math> is even, and all even numbers are divisible by two, which makes choices <math>A</math>, <math>C</math>, and <math>E</math> composite and not prime. 

Choice <math>D</math> also does not work since <math>999</math> is divisible by <math>9</math>, which means it's a composite number and not prime. Thus, the correct answer must be <math>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 996}</math>.

=== Solution 3 (Elimination) ===

The sum of the first <imath>n</imath> positive integers is <imath>\frac{(n)(n+1)}{2}</imath> and the product of the positive integers upto <imath>n</imath> is <imath>n!</imath>. The quotient of the two is -

<imath>\frac{(2)(n!)}{(n)(n+1)}</imath>

which simplifies to <imath>\frac{(2)((n-1)!)}{n+1}</imath>. Thus, <imath>n+1</imath> must be odd for the remainder to not be 0 (as <imath>2</imath> will multiply with some number in <imath>n!</imath>, cancelling out <imath>n+1</imath> if it is even, which leaves us with the answer choices <imath>n = 996</imath> and <imath>n = 998</imath>. Notice that <imath>n + 1</imath> must also be prime as otherwise there will be a factor of <imath>n + 1</imath> in <imath>2</imath> x <imath>n!</imath> somewhere. So either <imath>997</imath> or <imath>999</imath> must be prime - <imath>999</imath> is obviously not prime as it is divisible by 9, so our answer should be <imath>n</imath> where <imath>n + 1 = 997</imath>, and so our answer is <imath>n = 996</imath> or <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 996}</imath>.

- youtube.com/indianmathguy


=== Solution 4 (Trying the answer choices)===

The sum of the numbers from 1 through <imath>n</imath> is <imath>\frac{(n)(n+1)}{2}</imath>, and obviously, the products are the factorial; <imath>n!</imath>. We can try 995 first, where <imath>\frac{995(995+1)}{2}</imath> is the sum of the integers up to 995. This can be simplified to <imath>995 \cdot 498</imath>. Then we can set up an equation stating that <imath>995! = 995 \cdot 498 \cdot \mathbb{N}</imath>. (where <imath>\mathbb{N}</imath> is a number that would satisfy the equation as a natural number) Then we can cancel out 995 on each side, making it <imath>994! = 498 \cdot \mathbb{N}</imath>, or <imath>498 \mid 994!</imath>. Since 498 is a factor of 994, answer choice <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 995}</imath> is correct. 

So we move on to the next one, <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 996}</imath>

<imath>\frac{996(996+1)}{2}</imath> is the sum, and <imath>996!</imath> is the products. This makes it <imath>996! = 498 \cdot 997 \cdot \mathbb{N}</imath>. But then we can see that 997 is a prime number. In the expression <imath>996!</imath>, there is no 997 as a factor (since <imath>996!</imath> is <imath>1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot \cdots \cdot 995 \cdot 996</imath>, and there is clearly no 997 as a factor), making it so there is no natural number <imath>\mathbb{N}</imath> that satisfies the equation. So, we can conclude the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 996}</imath>

-Reddessiner (CCG2)
